source.title: Safe2Harm: Semantic Isomorphism Attacks for Jailbreaking Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study develops and evaluates its own semantic-isomorphism jailbreak attack against safety-aligned models. It does not test the fine-tuning, first-token, parameter-localization, shallowness, or deepening claims in the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Safe2Harm attack success rates, which bear on jailbreak vulnerability but do not test the particular mechanisms in V1–V7. It also compares other attack methods and evaluates harmful-content detectors; those results do not test a listed version. The main-text figure descriptions and the appendix tables contain additional attack results, but the flattened table layout does not reliably support assigning all values to their model and condition; only the clearly stated Llama-3-8B-Instruct results are recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-attack paper. Safe2Harm rewrites harmful questions into benign analogues, gets a detailed answer, then has the target model rewrite it back. It does not fine-tune models (V1/V2), measure per-token KL (V3), or prefill or use decoding changes (V4). It does not localize parameters (V5), explain shallowness (V6) or test deepening (V7). The original source (Qi et al.) is cited only as a GPT-4 judge method. The study neither tests nor builds on the shallow-alignment finding, so T6 fits better than T4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Safe2Harm achieves the best ASR in most scenarios across 7 LLMs without adversarial optimization. They also find that Qwen3Guard is the best harmful-content detector on their 358-sample dataset.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses semantic rewriting, topic mapping, safe-response generation, and inversion; it does not use the original sources' fine-tuning or token-distribution procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that Safe2Harm's ASR increases to some extent as Qwen3 model scale increases; they also report generally higher ASR for most attack methods in Qwen3 Thinking Mode than in standard mode.

fits_no_version.finding: Safe2Harm reaches 79.8–87.0% ASR on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct across three benchmarks. Its ASR is high on most of the 7 models (e.g. Gemini 2.5 Flash 97.98% on JailbreakBench).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rewriting harmful requests into principle-isomorphic benign requests, then inverting the answer, bypasses refusal in aligned LLMs.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3, Thinking Mode raises ASR for most attacks, and harmful responses go with longer thinking (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extended reasoning mode weakens refusal in reasoning-capable LLMs.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for attack success rates. The appendix tables are flattened in the supplied text, making some model-condition assignments unclear. The paper's own method is evaluated as an attack; the study does not test why safety behaviour may be shallow.
record.rows_left_out: Other attack-method results in Tables 2 and 4–6 were not extracted because they are comparisons to other methods rather than tests of a listed claim version; additional figure results are not stated as exact values in the text, and the flattened appendix layout does not reliably support assigning every value.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning is not done; fine-tuning is mentioned only as future work.
No per-token KL or other token-position analysis.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. GCG suffix attacks appear only as comparator baselines, without any position-level analysis.
No analysis of why alignment is shallow.

record.verdict_notes: Baseline GCG (suffix) ASRs on Llama-3-8B-Instruct are 29.5/20.5/44.0%, and on Qwen3-8B 2.5/0/5%. They are reported only as comparators, transferred to closed models, with no analysis of refusal depth. They could at most be weak V4-adjacent context and were not treated as a test. There are no uncertainty estimates. The ASR judge for the attack results is not clearly specified.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and changes in harmful-request compliance.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or selected benign data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Prefilling compliant opening tokens, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as ways to bypass refusal.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether training data or objectives cause safety behaviour to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety behaviour and whether that behaviour holds up.
